name: Vitamin D and K2 for teeth

image.caption: Vitamin D and K2 for teeth

lead: Some people take vitamins D and K2 hoping to help enamel and dentin remineralise and keep teeth strong-looking. The idea draws on the roles these vitamins play in bone mineralisation.

Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for osteocalcin, a protein involved in bone mineral formation. Clinical data on K2 for bone are described as inconclusive, and no studies of vitamins D and K2 for tooth remineralisation were found.

paras: They are taken as supplements or from foods such as fatty fish, egg yolks and fermented foods, usually as part of a broader nutrition-for-teeth approach alongside brushing and fluoride.
No dental-specific risks are documented. Vitamin K2 may interact with anticoagulants, so anyone on blood thinners would check with a clinician.

web.title: Vitamin D may help prevent dental caries

chain: Vitamins D and K2 support mineralisation
angle.text: Folk claims hold that vitamins D and K2 help teeth remineralise and rebuild, borrowing from bone research where K2 aids mineral formation. Dental trials of the idea have not been run.

lead: Vitamin D and vitamin K2 are discussed in dental-health circles as a pairing for stronger, better-mineralised teeth. The appearance chain proponents describe is that sturdier enamel and dentin mean fewer cavities, less wear and fewer chips, which helps keep teeth intact, white and good-looking. Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for osteocalcin, a protein involved in bone mineral formation, and proponents extend this mechanism from bone to teeth.[1]

Research on vitamin D and teeth is older and better developed than for K2. A systematic review by Philippe Hujoel of the University of Washington, published in Nutrition Reviews, pooled 24 controlled clinical trials in about 3,000 children, conducted between the 1920s and the 1980s, and associated raised vitamin D (through UV exposure or supplements such as cod-liver oil) with roughly a 50 percent reduction in tooth decay incidence.[2] Hujoel cautioned that the trials had weaknesses that could bias results and that participants lived in a very different era.[2]
No clinical studies of the combination of vitamin D and K2 for tooth remineralisation were found. Clinical data on K2 for bone are described as inconclusive.[1]

paras: Vitamin K2 activates vitamin K-dependent proteins such as osteocalcin; in vitro studies show effects on osteoblast differentiation, and bone effects may be stronger with vitamin D.[1] Application of these findings to teeth has not been established in clinical trials.

Tooth colour, enamel integrity and the absence of cavities and pits are part of how a smile looks, which is why people interested in appearance ask whether nutrition can strengthen teeth. The theory behind vitamins D and K2 runs in a chain: vitamin D supports calcium absorption, vitamin K2 is described as helping direct calcium to mineralised tissue, and sturdier mineralisation would mean teeth that resist decay and wear and therefore stay intact and bright for longer.[1][3][4] The links in that chain are drawn from bone and general-nutrition research; the step to visible tooth quality is the part proponents propose and that trials have not examined directly.

Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, about 96 percent mineral, mainly hydroxyapatite; mature enamel has no cells, blood vessels or nerves, so it cannot regrow once lost, although early surface damage can be repaired by remineralisation.[5] Fluoride helps calcium and phosphate rebuild the crystal surface, forming fluorapatite that resists acid better than the original enamel.[5] Enamel formation begins around the third or fourth month of pregnancy and proceeds at roughly 4 micrometres a day, in a secretory stage and a maturation stage.[5] Enamel hypoplasia, ranging from small pits to missing enamel, is a recognised defect category with several known causes.[5]

Vitamin D is a group of fat-soluble compounds that increase intestinal calcium absorption and help regulate blood calcium and phosphate for bone health. Most people obtain more from UVB skin exposure than from food; fatty fish, beef liver, eggs, cheese and UV-exposed mushrooms contain it, and milk and cereals are often fortified.[3] Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, and one review linked childhood deficiency to about a 22 percent higher risk of tooth decay.[3] Cod-liver oil was used folklorically in northern Europe, and the rickets-preventing factor was named vitamin D in 1922.[3] Excess raises blood calcium and can calcify soft tissues, though toxicity is rare and usually comes from high-dose supplements.[3]

Vitamin K covers K1 (phylloquinone), from leafy greens, and K2 (menaquinones), from animal foods and bacteria. MK-4 is made by animal tissues from K1, while MK-7 and longer forms come from bacteria, and natto, a fermented soybean food, is a rich source of MK-7.[4] The vitamin adds a calcium-binding group to proteins such as prothrombin and osteocalcin.[4] Vitamin K supplementation has produced mixed results on fracture risk, and short randomised trials found no clear effect on arterial calcification.[4] The anticoagulant warfarin blocks recycling of vitamin K, so changes in intake can affect its action.[4]

sections.h: Vitamin D and tooth decay research
paras: The Hujoel systematic review, published in Nutrition Reviews in late 2012, covered 24 controlled clinical trials in about 3,000 children aged 2 to 16, in which vitamin D status was raised by ultraviolet light or by supplements such as cod-liver oil; vitamin D was associated with roughly a 50 percent reduction in the incidence of decay.[2] In the accompanying press release, Hujoel cautioned that the trials had weaknesses that could have biased results and that the review should be interpreted carefully, while another researcher quoted in the release said the findings reaffirm the importance of vitamin D for dental health.[2] The release also noted that current reviews by bodies such as the Institute of Medicine and the American Dental Association had drawn no conclusions from this evidence.[2]
Whether declining vitamin D levels and rising childhood caries are connected remained open to debate, according to Hujoel.[2]

Dental reference material describes tooth decay as arising when demineralisation outpaces remineralisation, with saliva, fluoride and the frequency of sugar intake as the main established influences on remineralisation.[6]

sections.h: Historical background of diet and teeth
paras: The idea that diet governs tooth health has a long history. Wikipedia describes Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948), a Canadian-born dentist who chaired the National Dental Association from 1914 to 1928, as considering diet the main cause of tooth decay from 1894 and as suggesting in the early 1930s that vitamin B and mineral salts help prevent cavities.[7] His 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration compared the diets of groups including Swiss, Native American, Polynesian and Aboriginal communities and argued that refined flour, sugar and processed fats contributed to dental and general health problems, including crowded teeth.[7] Wikipedia also records that reviews of the book at the time were mixed, that a 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis questioned the picture of healthy traditional societies, and that the Weston A. Price Foundation continues to promote his work.[7]

The newer vitamin D and K2 discussion is a separate strand with its own literature: vitamin D was named in 1922 as the rickets-preventing factor associated with cod-liver oil, and the childhood caries trials analysed in 2012 used ultraviolet light and supplements such as cod-liver oil to raise vitamin D.[2][3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and wellness communities
paras: On T Nation, a poster recommended taking vitamin D with K2, saying K2 helps the body deposit vitamin D where it is needed, in bones and teeth, rather than in arteries.[8] Another thread participant said that lacking minerals in the diet does not by itself affect tooth enamel, reflecting disagreement about nutrient-based approaches to tooth health.[9]

No studies found on the combination of vitamin D and K2 for tooth remineralisation. The vitamin D evidence consists of the older childhood caries trials summarised in the 2012 systematic review of 24 trials, whose author noted possible biases in those trials.[2] Vitamin K research has centred on bone and blood clotting; Wikipedia notes mixed results for vitamin K supplementation and fracture risk and that short randomised trials found no clear effect on arterial calcification.[4]

lore.intro: Vitamin D plus K2 is mentioned in supplement discussions on fitness forums, usually as a package for bone, heart and tooth health.[8]

claims.claim: K2 directs vitamin D's calcium into bones and teeth and away from arteries.
Vitamin D plus K2 can remineralise or rebuild teeth
